blocks.text: **The problem.** Given an integer array `nums`, return `true` if there are three indexes `i < j < k` with `nums[i] < nums[j] < nums[k]` — three values that **increase** from left to right — and `false` otherwise. They don't need to be next to each other. The follow-up asks for **O(n) time and O(1) space**.

blocks.alt: The array [2, 1, 5, 0, 4, 6]. The values 1, 4 and 6 at indexes 1, 4 and 5 increase from left to right, so the answer is true.

elements.text: the three values may have other numbers between them
elements.originalText: the three values may have other numbers between them

blocks.code:
Input:  nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
Output: true       e.g. 1 < 2 < 3

Input:  nums = [5, 4, 3, 2, 1]
Output: false      the values only fall

Input:  nums = [2, 1, 5, 0, 4, 6]
Output: true       e.g. 1 < 4 < 6, or 0 < 4 < 6

blocks.text: 1. Brute force: try every triplet of indexes
Three nested loops check every `i < j < k` directly.
**Time O(n³), space O(1).** With up to 500,000 numbers, hopeless.
2. Optimal: think about the middle element

Fix the **middle** value `nums[j]`. A triplet exists around it if something **smaller** appears before it and something **bigger** appears after it. The best candidates are simply the **smallest value to its left** and the **largest value to its right** — and both can be precomputed for every index in one pass each.

blocks.alt: For [2, 1, 5, 0, 4, 6]: the smallest value up to each index is [2, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0] and the largest value from each index to the end is [6, 6, 6, 6, 6, 6]. At index 2, the smallest value before it is 1 and the largest after it is 6, and 1 < 5 < 6.
blocks.caption: nums[j] can be the middle when minLeft[j − 1] < nums[j] < maxRight[j + 1].

blocks.text: **Time O(n), space O(n).** Linear — but two extra arrays, and the follow-up asks for O(1) space.
3. Best solution: keep the two smallest "starters"
Walk once and keep just two numbers:

items: `second` — the smallest value seen so far that has something **smaller before it**. In other words, the end of the best increasing pair.

blocks.text: For each `x`: if `x ≤ first`, it becomes the new `first`. Otherwise, if `x ≤ second`, it becomes the new `second` (a better, lower pair end). Otherwise `x` is bigger than `second` — and `second` has a smaller value before it — so we have a triplet.

The surprising part: `first` can move to an index **after** `second`. That's fine. `second` still remembers that *some* smaller value came before it; the new `first` is just a better start for future pairs.

blocks.alt: A trace of first and second on [20, 100, 10, 12, 5, 13]. first becomes 20, then second 100, then first 10, then second 12, then first 5 (now after second), and finally 13 is bigger than second = 12, so the answer is true: 10 < 12 < 13.
blocks.caption: When 13 arrives, second = 12 still remembers that 10 came before it: 10 < 12 < 13.
Try the "Tricky" example, where first jumps past second, and a strictly decreasing array, where second never gets set.

blocks.text: **Time O(n), space O(1).** One pass, two variables. The `≤` comparisons matter: with `<`, an array like `[1, 1, 1]` would wrongly report a triplet.

blocks.alt: Brute force: O(n³) time, O(1) space. Optimal: O(n) time, O(n) space. Best: O(n) time, O(1) space.

items: **Equal values** — `[1, 1, 1, 1]` is `false`: the triplet must be strictly increasing.

blocks.text: Keeping "the smallest possible end for an increasing run of length 1, 2, …" is the core of the O(n log n) **Longest Increasing Subsequence** algorithm — this problem is its length-3 special case.
